title: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (5 of 7)
hook: the first roti off the pan isn't for anyone at the table
tomorrow: Karma yoga deep-dive: action as offering; Karma Yoga as taught by Vivekananda; work as worship (6 of 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the woman at the door and the vyadha, the butcher in the market. Duty, done with care, is worship.

In a lot of Hindu kitchens, something small happens before anyone eats. The first roti comes off the pan, or the first spoon of rice from the pot, and it doesn't go to the hungriest kid. It goes on a little plate in front of the family's shrine, or to the cow outside, or to the birds on the wall. Then everyone eats. Nobody thinks the gods are starving. The cooking, which could have been just a chore, has been turned toward something. Today: the verse that turns a whole day of work the same way.
screen: `THE FIRST ROTI OFF THE PAN.` → `NOT FOR THE HUNGRIEST KID.` → `WORK, TURNED TOWARD SOMETHING.`

segments.voice: Near the very end of the Bhagavad Gita, in chapter eighteen, Krishna gives a line karma yoga leans on more than almost any other. Paraphrased: the one from whom all beings come, by whom all this is spread out, worshiping that one with your own work, a person reaches perfection. Svakarmana tam abhyarcya. With your own work, worship. Not someone else's work. Not a special holy job you'll get around to someday. Your own: the teacher's lesson plan, the nurse's night shift, the accountant's spreadsheet, done honestly. In chapter nine Krishna says it even more plainly: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer, whatever you give, whatever effort you make, do it as an offering to me. Vivekananda pushed this into the street. For him the offering had a face. Serve people as you would serve God, he taught, because God is in them. That idea became the motto of the order he founded in 1897, the Ramakrishna Mission: for your own freedom, and for the good of the world. And chapter two has a line that shows what offered work looks like from the outside: yoga is skill in action. Offered work isn't sloppy work done with a holy feeling. It's careful. Nobody offers a burnt roti on purpose.
screen: `WITH YOUR OWN WORK, WORSHIP.` · `WHATEVER YOU DO, AS AN OFFERING.` · `SERVE PEOPLE AS YOU'D SERVE GOD.` · `YOGA IS SKILL IN ACTION.` · then, large: `OFFER THE WORK.`

segments.voice: Picture the first real task waiting for you after this, your hands on the keyboard, the wheel, the dishes or the lesson plan, and notice how you usually meet it: rushed, bored, braced. Now picture doing that same task with care, as if someone you love were going to receive it. If you pray, dedicate it silently, the way the first roti goes to the shrine; if you don't, just let it be done well, for its own sake.
Svakarmana, with one's own work. Work as worship: with your own work, worship. Offered work is careful work.
Your line: offer the work. Yoga is skill in action. Two hundred sixty-four days, and counting.

howItsDone: Many Hindu households offer the first portion of cooked food at the home shrine, or to a cow or birds, before the family eats; the Ramakrishna Mission and many seva groups describe service to people as worship.

fork.setup: you're dreading a dull report at work. using the Gita's chapter nine, what does karma yoga suggest?
options: do it as an offering, and do it well.
do it fast and badly: it doesn't matter.
fork.reveal: whatever you do, do it as an offering, says 9.27. and 2.50 adds: yoga is skill in action.

original.note: Sanskrit, Gita 18.46: 'with one's own work, worshiping that one.' sva (own) + karmanā (by work); abhyarcya, having worshiped.

trapdoor: what you thought: worship happens in a temple, and work happens at work.
what it means: the Gita says your own work, offered, is worship.
what a scholar hears: svakarmaṇā in 18.46 ties worship to one's own varṇa duties in the chapter's context; modern teachers like Vivekananda widened it to all honest work and to service of people.
guess: worshiping God through the work that is yours
the karma your past deeds have earned you
giving up your job to serve in a temple
